vignette: The elevator doors slide shut behind her on a Tuesday in November. She is leaving the downtown server farm, carrying an insulated coffee cup and her daily crossword. At sixty-six, she expects routine. Instead, the man who steps in does not speak at first. He presses the button for the sub-basement. When the car drops, he turns. She feels the weight of his proximity, the damp wool of his coat, the sudden shift in the air. He takes what he wants. Eleven minutes stretch into an eternity. She remembers his scent, the way her own voice fractures when she says no, the metallic click of the doors opening on the concrete floor. She walks out without calling anyone. She takes the service stairs down, crosses three wet streets, and buys a flashlight she does not need. In the days that follow, she cannot sleep unless the television glows in the corner. Her body learns to brace before the doors close. She abandons public transit, then avoids subways, then avoids any elevator that rattles. Tama dies four years ago from heart failure, and without him to check the peephole, the apartment grows heavier. She locks the deadbolt three times. When neighbors knock, she presses her ear to the wood, counting footsteps in her head. She tells herself it is simply caution. She tells herself it is aging. Her life as a network engineer is built on architecture and uptime. She maps fiber optic pathways and debugs corrupted packets in the quiet hours before dawn. Her desk holds dual monitors, a mechanical keyboard, and three photographs of her and Tama standing on a Rarotonga shore. At sixty-six, she thought she had outgrown the need for certainty. She prides herself on precision, on tracing the invisible connections that keep systems alive. But the code shifts under her fingers. When a server drops offline, she does not run diagnostics immediately. She sits back, watches the ceiling, and waits for someone to enter the room. Her pulse hammers against her collarbone. She starts every shift by checking the building security feed, not because her department requires it, but because she needs to know who occupies the seventh floor. Colleagues notice she no longer stays for afternoon stand-ups. She logs off by 4:30, takes the stairs down the stairwell, and walks the perimeter of the block twice before heading home. The work still makes sense. The problem is the world outside the screen, where connections fracture without warning. She wakes at 2:14 a.m. most nights, her sheets tangled around her ankles. The dream arrives without warning: the elevator descending, a shadow stretching across the ceiling, the sudden pressure of a hand on her shoulder. She stops fighting it now. She simply lies still until her breathing slows. During daylight hours, she moves through the city with deliberate economy. She shops at the same hour, sits in the corner booth, keeps her bag between her feet and the window. When a man raises his voice on the street, she crosses to the opposite sidewalk, her shoulders tight, her vision narrowing to the pavement. She tells her therapist, in the quiet pauses between sessions, that she used to love the sound of rain. Now it only pulls her back to that Tuesday, to the damp wool, to the way she stopped trusting locks altogether. The city hums around her, but she stands apart, watching the doors, waiting for the next drop. Her hands rest on the keyboard, fingers hovering over the keys, tracing the familiar layout while her mind scans the room for exits, for threats, for the invisible wire that might snap before the next reset. She breathes in, counts to four, and waits for the silence to pass.
